articleSummary: White-spotted and star-marked midges (蛾蚋) are small Diptera widely distributed across China. Adults live about 15 days. In urban areas, the white-spotted and star-marked midge larvae develop in shallow waters rich in decaying organic matter, including septic tanks, sewage pools, toilets, and outdoor clogged drainage or other standing-water containers. Females lay eggs in bathrooms, kitchens, drains, or water-holding containers. The larval stage lasts 14–16 days, followed by 3–4 days as pupae before adults emerge. Adults and larvae can perch on white-painted or ceramic walls, reducing perceived cleanliness. These larvae can cause myiasis (fly maggot infestation) if they accidentally enter a host, exploiting host tissue to complete development; such myiasis is generally linked to poor wound care and disinfection, representing a facultative parasitic occurrence. No case counts or outbreaks are reported; the text highlights domestic exposure risks in China.

articleHeadline: Biological Warfare Waged Against Dengue Mosquito
articleSummary: Dengue, transmitted by Aedes aegypti, affects an estimated 390 million people globally each year. With no specific treatment, prevention is essential; conventional vector control has fallen short. The Wolbachia method infects mosquitoes with a natural bacterium and releases Wolbachia-infected individuals to supplant native Aedes aegypti, blocking dengue transmission. Successful in Brazil’s Joinville and Singapore, it has reduced disease risk. In Joinville, an Endemic Control Agent releases about 200 Wolbachia mosquitoes four days weekly, protecting roughly 75% of Joinville's 600,000 residents; early results show dengue deaths dropped to zero. In Singapore, dengue cases declined 87.6% during 2022–2025, and by August 2026 only one dengue death occurred (vs 32 in 2020). The program targets about 800,000 households by October 2026 at US$31.4 million/year, with 72,000 traps weekly and up to 10 million male mosquitoes weekly from Google. Guangzhou and Malaysia with Serum Institute vaccine trials illustrate broader regional efforts.

articleSummary: Severe dengue fever in a 23-year-old pregnant woman in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, required four major interventions. In early August, at 39 weeks, N.T.M.L., a Đồng Nai resident, developed high fever and dengue. She delivered by cesarean, but postpartum hemorrhage with severe coagulopathy and acute liver failure progressed to shock and multiorgan failure. Upon transfer to Gia Định People's Hospital, she was comatose, hypotensive, intubated, and on mechanical ventilation; platelets were critically low and coagulation severely deranged. A multidisciplinary team provided aggressive resuscitation, transfusions, plasma exchange, liver support, infection control, and eventually a hysterectomy to control bleeding. She then underwent endovascular embolization to stop ongoing bleeding, avoiding further open surgery. After more than 15 days, she is awake, breathing independently, eating, and preparing for discharge. The report stresses close monitoring of dengue in pregnancy, especially days 3–7, and sustained vector control. In Ho Chi Minh City, dengue cases exceed 25,700 year-to-date.

articleHeadline: H1N1 can affect the eyes too. Watch for these warning signs as flu surges
articleSummary: As of 26 August 2026, Delhi reports nearly 2,500 confirmed H1N1 cases this year and about 650 other influenza cases, with total flu infections surpassing 3,000 and influenza-like illness affecting Delhi-NCR and several other cities. H1N1 mainly causes respiratory illness but can occasionally involve the eyes; the common finding is viral conjunctivitis with redness, watering, burning and eyelid swelling, sometimes with mild discharge and light sensitivity. Severe coughing or vomiting can cause a subconjunctival haemorrhage. Rarely, deeper structures—uvea, retina or optic nerve—may be inflamed, presenting as uveitis, retinitis or optic neuritis and risking vision. Red flags include persistent blurred vision, severe eye pain, marked light sensitivity, sudden vision loss, floaters, or diplopia; any new vision change during influenza warrants ophthalmic assessment. Prevention centers on vaccination, hand hygiene, coughing etiquette, avoiding close contact, and staying home when ill; avoid touching eyes and sharing towels or lenses, and seek care for symptoms.

articleSummary: As of 26 August 2026, São Paulo confirmed two initial human West Nile fever cases in Ribeirão Preto and São José do Rio Preto. In Santa Catarina, two additional cases were confirmed in Imbituba and Caçador, with one patient dying. West Nile fever is an arbovirus infection transmitted mainly by Culex mosquitoes active at dawn and dusk; birds are reservoirs. Humans and horses are incidental hosts and not the main source. Human-to-human transmission is rare, occurring via blood transfusion, organ transplant, or mother-to-child during pregnancy or breastfeeding. About 80% of infections are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, illness resembles a virose with fever, headache, muscle and joint pains, nausea, fatigue, and rash. Less than 1% develop neurological disease such as meningitis or encephalitis, more likely in elderly and those with chronic diseases. Diagnosis relies on serology or RT-PCR, though cross-reactivity with dengue, Zika, and yellow fever can complicate confirmation.

articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola virus infection treated in Berlin: A 39-year-old US physician contracted Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo while caring for a patient and was evacuated to Charité Berlin (May 20–June 6) for an experimental therapy. The regimen combined MBP134, two monoclonal antibodies against Ebolaviruses, with remdesivir and intensive supportive care. Initial viral loads were very high but declined; by day 13 (nine days after treatment start) no viral RNA was detectable in blood, throat, urine, or stool, with semen turning negative by day 25. Genomic sequencing linked the virus to current outbreak strains but distinguished it from 2007/2012 Bundibugyo viruses, suggesting recent zoonotic spillover. The patient recovered and was discharged 22 days after symptom onset. MBP134 elicited neutralizing antibodies, and a host antibody response was detected despite therapy. Five household contacts (wife and four children) received MBP134 (50 mg/kg) as postexposure prophylaxis on days 5–6 after last exposure. A WHO-funded PARTNERS trial compares Remdesivir, MBP134, and their combination.

They engineered a genetically modified chikungunya virus that can replicate only once in the host, providing a precise and safe immune stimulus without causing disease. This platform advances vaccine technology beyond whole-virus or nucleic-acid approaches, aiming to improve safety across populations.

articleSummary: Schistosomiasis transmission in China depends on the snail Oncomelania hupensis. A National Institute of Parasitic Diseases study combines a 45-day temperature experiment with surveillance from 34,554 villages across 12 provinces (1990–2022) to assess warming effects on snail survival and density. articleSummary: An interinstitutional team led by the University of California, Riverside, and USAMRIID identifies new antibody targets on Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever virus (CCHFV), a tick-borne infection with up to 40% case fatality and no highly effective approved treatments. Published in Nature Communications, the study targets the viral nucleocapsid (NP) protein, an internal component that protects the genome. Four NP binding sites were identified; antibodies protected mice whether binding the NP head or stalk. The strongest antibody, 9D5, conferred protection from lethal infection and showed cross-strain potential, aided by X-ray structures of head-region binding. NP is not on the virion surface but can appear on infected cell surfaces, enabling TRIM21-mediated intracellular immune activation by non-neutralizing antibodies. Findings support antibody cocktails and humanized versions for broad protection. CCHFV occurs across eastern/southern Europe, NW China, Central Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and the Indian subcontinent, with expanding tick ranges increasing exposure risk and potential healthcare transmission.

articleSummary: Emerging infectious diseases can appear suddenly and threaten health; prevention hinges on public measures and individual actions. Full vaccination protects against measles, influenza, chickenpox, diphtheria, pertussis, hepatitis B, COVID-19, and pneumococcal disease. Hand hygiene with soap and water is essential; if unavailable, use sanitizer with ≥60% alcohol. Wear masks to reduce respiratory spread, especially when symptomatic or caring for patients; ensure good ventilation. Cover coughs/sneezes with tissue or elbow; dispose of tissues and wash hands. Practice safe food handling: cook thoroughly, use clean water, keep raw and cooked foods separate, and avoid undercooked animal products. Avoid wildlife and sick animals; report unusual animal deaths. Prevent vectors by removing standing water, covering containers, nets, and repellents, especially where dengue and Zika circulate. Seek prompt medical care for high fever, breathing difficulty, severe symptoms, or dehydration, and follow health authorities. A healthy lifestyle supports immunity but cannot replace vaccines or targeted defenses.

articleSummary: Malaria, caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, remains a major global threat: over 280 million infections and about 610,000 deaths annually, endemic in 80 countries, with non-endemic areas facing importation risks from travel. Recent focus centers on Germany’s Frankfurt airport, where two deaths and four positive cases were reported. In Africa, 94% of cases and 95% of deaths occur, with children under five accounting for roughly 75% of deaths there. Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and Ethiopia together contribute about half of global cases; Nigeria alone accounts for 38.6% of under-5 deaths. Global incidence fell 2000–2015 but rose ~8.5% by 2024; 2024 incidence rose 2% vs 2023 (64 vs 62.7 per 1,000 in risk areas). Symptoms range from fever and headache to severe fatigue, confusion, seizures, and respiratory distress. Prevention includes insecticide-treated nets and indoor spraying; rising insecticide resistance challenges gains. WHO-recommended RTS,S/AS01 vaccine (since 2021) and R21/Matrix-M (since 2023) are being rolled out in Africa, with potential to save tens of thousands of lives yearly. Treatments rely on artemisinin-based combinations; chloroquine remains for sensitive P. vivax; primaquine adds to prevent relapses.

articleSummary: West Nile fever has arrived in Brazil, with four confirmed cases this week: two in São Paulo state (Ribeirão Preto and São José do Rio Preto) and two in Santa Catarina (Caçador and Imbituba), including a 77-year-old woman who died on August 8. The virus, transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, causes symptoms in about 20% of infections, such as abrupt fever, malaise, loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, eye pain, headache, muscle pain, and a maculopapular rash with lymphadenopathy; severe cases affect the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis or meningitis, neck stiffness, confusion, weakness, paralysis, seizures, or coma. Overall mortality is low, but around 10% in CNS involvement. Diagnosis relies on clinical and laboratory assessment; there is no vaccine or specific antiviral—treatment is supportive, with hospitalization or ICU for severe cases. Elderly and those with hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, transplants, or immunobiological therapy are higher-risk. Originating in Uganda (1937), the virus spread globally via migratory birds and reached Brazil in 2026, with climate change cited as a driver of arboviral dissemination.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Rapid test for the West Nile virus is coming.
articleHeadline: Έρχεται rapid τεστ για τον ιό του Δυτικού Νείλου
articleSummary: By 2026-08-27, a Greek research team at the University of Athens is developing a rapid point-of-care test that detects West Nile virus and three other arboviruses (Zika, Dengue fever, and Chikungunya) from a single drop of blood using graphene biosensors for differential diagnosis, aiming to reduce misdiagnoses. The project SURVIVE-VBD, funded by EU4Health with a 4 million euro budget, includes Greece alongside Italy, Spain, Estonia, the Netherlands, and Brazil. Lead Greek investigator is Professor Maria Gazouli. A second component will pair test results with environmental data in an AI model to issue risk area alerts for preventive action. Greece faces a summer surge of West Nile virus activity, centered in Attica with about 39 municipalities at risk; no domestic Zika, Dengue, or Chikungunya cases reported yet, though imported cases exist. If adopted, MOH and EODY could roll out tests via mobile health units within 36 months.

articleHeadlineTranslated: WHO: The Ebola outbreak in Uganda has ended, while in DR Congo it is still ongoing.
articleHeadline: СЗО: Епидемијата на ебола во Уганда заврши, во ДР Конго сè уште трае
articleSummary: Uganda's Ebola outbreak has ended, with 20 cases and 2 deaths, according to the Ugandan government on July 28 and later confirmed by the WHO. The WHO monitored to ensure no hidden transmission chains. In neighboring DR Congo, the outbreak remains ongoing and highly active. Government figures show more than 5,600 infections and over 2,700 deaths as of Tuesday. Transmission continues at a high level, though some slowing in growth has been noted. Marie-Roseline Belizer, WHO Regional Director for Emergency Preparedness in Africa, said contact tracing and testing have improved, and analyses of the Bundibugyo ebolavirus show no signs of mutation despite rapid spread. However, a funding shortfall of about $30 million for logistics, including medical and personal protective equipment, threatens operations in the hardest-hit Congo areas. Without investment, momentum could be lost.

locations: Ituri; Democratic Republic of the Congo; Republic of Uganda
articleHeadline: A Hundred Days In, Congo's Ebola Outbreak Is Still Getting Bigger
articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has grown to 5,656 confirmed cases and 2,715 deaths as of 24 August, the largest Ebola epidemic in DR Congo and the second largest anywhere. In the last day, 72 new confirmed cases and 35 deaths were recorded. Ituri accounts for 4,716 cases and 2,119 deaths; North Kivu 735. The outbreak spans 58 of 151 health zones across six provinces. There is no approved vaccine or treatment for Bundibugyo; Ervebo against Zaire strain may offer some protection, but evidence is uncertain. About 70,000 doses released: 20,000 for a trial, 50,000 for frontline workers with informed consent. As of 9 August, 155 health workers infected, 45 dead; ~792 in isolation, 1,245 recovered. WHO recommends restricting mass gatherings, road and boat surveillance, and road checkpoints; border closures not advised. Uganda: 20 cases, 2 deaths; outbreak declared over on 28 July.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Tangerang City Now Has the Lung Friends Healthy House to Treat TB.
articleHeadline: Kota Tangerang Kini Miliki Rumah Sehat Sahabat Paru untuk Tangani TBC
articleSummary: Rumah Sehat BAZNAS Sahabat Paru (Lung Friends Healthy House) in Tangerang City, Indonesia, opens to support tuberculosis (TB) patients, particularly those with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). On August 27, 2026, the facility was inaugurated in a cross-sector collaboration among the Tangerang City Government, BAZNAS Kota Tangerang, and the City Health Office, and is the first program of its kind in Banten Province. The program is funded by BAZNAS, with beneficiary selection and treatment coaching conducted alongside the Health Office. The house offers three rooms for up to six patients, with 14 days of accompaniment and medication per patient. The program aims to improve treatment adherence, cut transmission to families and communities, and help patients return to health and independence, potentially with post-recovery economic support to start small businesses. Staff include public health workers, cadres, primary care professionals, and pulmonary specialists.

articleHeadline: Delhi H1N1 Alert: 138 New Cases In 24 Hours, Hospitals Told To Stay Fully Prepared
articleSummary: Delhi records 138 new H1N1 cases in 24 hours, total 2,446, with Influenza-A reaching 3,177. Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh led a virtual review with Medical Directors and Medical Superintendents, supported by the Health Secretary, to bolster Delhi hospital preparedness for a potential surge in influenza and respiratory diseases. Hospitals must maintain five isolation beds each (ten in larger facilities), establish flu corners for emergencies, and enforce round-the-clock duty rosters for staff. Senior residents should cover emergency duties; samples can be collected for testing and there must be adequate viral transport medium (VTM). Maintain sufficient medicine stocks and pursue local procurement to ensure continuity. IEC materials should inform patients about symptoms and treatment. Officials urged vigilance, not panic, emphasizing respiratory hygiene, masks, and prompt medical consultation for vulnerable groups.
